text:
# Production Runbook
For: Laravel 10 app on PHP 8.2-FPM, nginx, MySQL 8.0, Hetzner Cloud  
Audience: Two PHP developers with basic Linux familiarity  
Goal: Keep production running safely for the next 6 months with no platform change and no extra monthly tooling cost.

---

## 0) What this runbook is for

This runbook tells you how to:

- check whether production is healthy
- restart services safely
- deploy the Laravel app
- verify backups
- restore from backup
- renew/verify TLS certificates
- handle common incidents
- know when to stop and escalate

If something is not covered here, stop and escalate rather than guessing.

---

# 1) Environment overview

## Servers

### `app-1`
- Ubuntu Linux
- nginx
- PHP 8.2-FPM
- Laravel 10 app
- queue worker managed by Supervisor
- certbot / Let’s Encrypt
- Uptime Kuma

### `db-1`
- Ubuntu Linux
- MySQL 8.0
- cron job for nightly `mysqldump`
- rclone uploads backups to Backblaze B2
- 14 daily copies retained

---

## 2) Access and credentials

### You must have
- SSH access to both servers
- sudo access on both servers
- access to the production app repository
- access to the Hetzner Cloud console
- access to Backblaze B2 bucket credentials/config on `db-1`
- access to the Telegram alert group, if needed for incident confirmation
- Laravel `.env` file on `app-1` location known
- MySQL root or admin credentials on `db-1`

### Never do
- Never edit production directly without a backup or rollback plan
- Never reboot both servers at once
- Never change firewall rules without confirming SSH access remains open
- Never modify database settings without a backup first
- Never “just test” things in production without understanding impact

---

# 3) Standard login commands

Replace `USER`, `APP1_IP`, `DB1_IP` with real values.

```bash
ssh USER@APP1_IP
ssh USER@DB1_IP
```

If you need sudo:

```bash
sudo -i
```

Check who you are:

```bash
whoami
hostname
```

Expected:
- `hostname` should show either `app-1` or `db-1`
- `whoami` should be your user or `root` only after `sudo -i`

---

# 4) Normal daily health check

Do this every working day, or at least before and after deployments.

## 4.1 Check the app server

SSH to `app-1`, then run:

```bash
systemctl status nginx --no-pager
systemctl status php8.2-fpm --no-pager
systemctl status supervisor --no-pager
systemctl status certbot.timer --no-pager
```

What success looks like:
- all services show `active (running)` or `active (waiting)` for the timer
- no repeated failures in the status output

Check disk space:

```bash
df -h
```

What success looks like:
- root filesystem and `/var` are not near full
- if any filesystem is above 80%, investigate

Check app logs for obvious errors:

```bash
tail -n 50 /var/log/nginx/error.log
journalctl -u php8.2-fpm -n 50 --no-pager
journalctl -u supervisor -n 50 --no-pager
```

If Laravel logs are stored in the project, also check:

```bash
tail -n 50 /path/to/app/storage/logs/laravel.log
```

What success looks like:
- no repeated fatal errors
- occasional old warnings are fine if the app is behaving normally

---

## 4.2 Check the database server

SSH to `db-1`, then run:

```bash
systemctl status mysql --no-pager
systemctl status cron --no-pager
df -h
```

What success looks like:
- MySQL is `active (running)`
- cron is `active (running)`
- disk is not near full

Check MySQL is responsive:

```bash
mysqladmin ping -uroot -p
```

Expected:
- `mysqld is alive`

If you do not know the root password or it is stored elsewhere, use the documented admin credentials your team has saved.

---

## 4.3 Check backup status

On `db-1`, inspect cron and recent backups:

```bash
ls -lh /path/to/backup/directory | tail
```

Check the backup script output location if one exists, for example:

```bash
cat /var/log/backup.log
```

If rclone is used manually or via script, test listing the bucket:

```bash
rclone lsd b2:BUCKET_NAME
```

Or list recent objects:

```bash
rclone ls b2:BUCKET_NAME | tail
```

What success looks like:
- nightly dump file exists for last night
- upload succeeded
- you can see roughly 14 recent daily copies retained

If the backup for last night is missing, treat this as an incident.

---

# 5) How to check the live site

From your laptop or from `app-1`, use:

```bash
curl -I https://yourdomain.com
```

Success looks like:
- `HTTP/2 200` or `HTTP/1.1 200`
- or another expected application response like `302` redirect to login

Then do a page fetch:

```bash
curl -s https://yourdomain.com | head
```

If you have a health endpoint, use it:

```bash
curl -s https://yourdomain.com/health
```

Success looks like:
- valid response from the app
- no TLS errors
- no timeout

---

# 6) Deploying the Laravel app

## 6.1 Before you deploy

Make sure:
- you know what commit or branch you are deploying
- database migrations are understood
- you have a rollback plan
- the site is currently healthy

Optional but recommended:
- announce a short maintenance window if the change is risky
- take a quick backup of current `.env` and current release state if your deploy process uses releases

---

## 6.2 If deployment is just `git pull`

SSH to `app-1` and go to the app directory:

```bash
cd /path/to/app
git status
git pull
```

Success looks like:
- clean pull or fast-forward update
- no merge conflicts

Install/update dependencies if needed:

```bash
composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
```

If frontend assets are part of your deploy process and built on-server:

```bash
npm ci
npm run build
```

Only do this if the server already has the required node toolchain installed and this is part of the known process.

Run migrations only if the release requires them:

```bash
php artisan migrate --force
```

Success looks like:
- migrations complete without error

Clear and rebuild caches if that is your standard process:

```bash
php artisan config:clear
php artisan route:clear
php artisan view:clear
php artisan cache:clear
php artisan config:cache
php artisan route:cache
php artisan view:cache
```

If you know your app breaks on cached routes or config, follow the team’s agreed pattern. If not sure, use the above only if this is already standard practice.

Restart PHP-FPM:

```bash
sudo systemctl restart php8.2-fpm
```

Restart queue worker if needed:

```bash
sudo supervisorctl restart all
```

Or if only one program is configured, restart that program specifically.

Check status:

```bash
systemctl status php8.2-fpm --no-pager
sudo supervisorctl status
```

Then verify the site:

```bash
curl -I https://yourdomain.com
```

Success looks like:
- app responds normally
- no new errors in logs
- queue worker is running

---

## 6.3 If your deployment uses a release directory and symlink

If the team uses `/var/www/releases/...` and a `current` symlink, only follow the documented pattern already in place. A typical safe pattern is:

1. create new release directory
2. checkout code
3. install dependencies
4. run migrations if needed
5. switch symlink
6. reload services

Example pattern:

```bash
cd /var/www/releases
mkdir -p "$(date +%F-%H%M%S)"
cd "$(ls -1dt */ | head -n 1)"
git pull
composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
php artisan migrate --force
ln -sfn /var/www/releases/NEW_RELEASE /var/www/current
sudo systemctl reload nginx
sudo systemctl restart php8.2-fpm
sudo supervisorctl restart all
```

Only use this if it matches the existing setup. If not, stop and ask the previous owner or inspect existing deploy scripts.

---

# 7) How to verify deployment succeeded

After a deploy, check all of the following:

## 7.1 Web response
```bash
curl -I https://yourdomain.com
```

Success:
- `200`, `302`, or expected response code

## 7.2 App logs
```bash
tail -n 50 /path/to/app/storage/logs/laravel.log
tail -n 50 /var/log/nginx/error.log
journalctl -u php8.2-fpm -n 50 --no-pager
```

Success:
- no new fatal errors
- no repeated permission issues
- no DB connection failures

## 7.3 Queue worker
```bash
sudo supervisorctl status
```

Success:
- worker shows `RUNNING`

## 7.4 Uptime Kuma
Open Uptime Kuma and verify monitors are green. If Telegram alerts fired during deploy, confirm they have stopped after recovery.

---

# 8) Queue worker operations

If jobs are stuck or failed due to a deploy, you may need to restart the worker.

On `app-1`:

```bash
sudo supervisorctl status
sudo supervisorctl restart all
```

If only one process exists, restart that specific process:

```bash
sudo supervisorctl restart laravel-worker
```

Success:
- process returns to `RUNNING`

If the queue is still not processing:
- check Laravel logs
- check Supervisor config
- check if Redis or another queue backend is running if used
- escalate if unresolved

---

# 9) MySQL operations

## 9.1 Check MySQL health

On `db-1`:

```bash
systemctl status mysql --no-pager
mysqladmin ping -uroot -p
```

If you know a non-root SQL user for monitoring:

```bash
mysql -uUSER -p -e "SELECT 1;"
```

Success:
- MySQL is running
- simple query returns `1`

---

## 9.2 Safe restart of MySQL

Only restart MySQL if it is hung, crash-looping, or required after maintenance.

Before restarting:
- confirm application impact
- expect brief downtime for database-dependent parts of the app

Command:

```bash
sudo systemctl restart mysql
```

Check:

```bash
systemctl status mysql --no-pager
mysqladmin ping -uroot -p
```

Success:
- MySQL active
- ping returns alive

If restart fails, stop and escalate.

---

# 10) Backups

## 10.1 What the backup system does

Nightly cron on `db-1`:
- runs `mysqldump`
- creates a backup file
- uploads it to Backblaze B2 via `rclone`
- keeps 14 daily copies

---

## 10.2 Check the backup script

Find the cron entry:

```bash
crontab -l
sudo crontab -l
ls -l /etc/cron.*
```

Check the script file and read it:

```bash
cat /path/to/backup-script.sh
```

What success looks like:
- it uses `mysqldump`
- it creates a dated file
- it uploads to B2 using `rclone`
- it removes old backups older than 14 days, if that is part of the process

---

## 10.3 Verify latest backup exists locally

On `db-1`:

```bash
ls -lh /path/to/backup/directory | tail -n 5
```

Look for a backup file from last night.

Success:
- file exists
- size is reasonable and not zero

---

## 10.4 Verify upload to Backblaze B2

```bash
rclone ls b2:BUCKET_NAME | tail -n 20
```

or

```bash
rclone lsf b2:BUCKET_NAME --max-depth 1
```

Success:
- most recent backup is present
- old backups still present up to 14 daily copies

---

## 10.5 Run a manual backup

If the automated backup failed, you can run it manually.

Example:

```bash
bash /path/to/backup-script.sh
```

If the script is executable:

```bash
/path/to/backup-script.sh
```

Success:
- a new dump file is created
- upload succeeds
- script exits with code 0

Check exit code:

```bash
echo $?
```

Success:
- `0`

---

# 11) Restoring from backup

Only restore if necessary and only after confirming the latest good backup.

## 11.1 When to restore
Use restore if:
- database is corrupted
- data was accidentally deleted
- app is unusable and DB is the cause
- a bad migration needs rollback and backup restore is the safe path

Do not restore just because the app is slow. Investigate first.

---

## 11.2 Restore procedure overview

High level:
1. choose the right backup
2. stop app writes
3. restore dump to MySQL
4. verify tables and app behavior
5. restart app services

If possible, notify the team before restoring because data may be lost after the backup point.

---

## 11.3 Download backup from Backblaze B2

On `db-1`, identify the backup object:

```bash
rclone ls b2:BUCKET_NAME | tail -n 20
```

Copy the exact backup you want, for example:

```bash
rclone copy b2:BUCKET_NAME/path/to/backup.sql.gz /tmp/restore/
```

Success:
- file downloads successfully

---

## 11.4 Restore the dump

If compressed:

```bash
gunzip -c /tmp/restore/backup.sql.gz | mysql -uroot -p DATABASE_NAME
```

If plain SQL:

```bash
mysql -uroot -p DATABASE_NAME < /tmp/restore/backup.sql
```

Success:
- command finishes without errors
- MySQL prompt returns

If the database must be dropped and recreated, do that only if you are certain:

```bash
mysql -uroot -p
```

Inside MySQL:

```sql
DROP DATABASE DATABASE_NAME;
CREATE DATABASE DATABASE_NAME CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
EXIT;
```

Then import again.

---

## 11.5 Verify restore

Run:

```bash
mysql -uroot -p -e "USE DATABASE_NAME; SHOW TABLES;"
```

Then verify app behavior through the website and logs.

Success:
- tables exist
- app loads
- no fatal DB errors

---

# 12) TLS / Let’s Encrypt

Certbot runs on `app-1`.

## 12.1 Check certificate status

```bash
sudo certbot certificates
```

Success:
- certificate listed
- expiry date is in the future

Check renewal timer:

```bash
systemctl status certbot.timer --no-pager
```

Success:
- timer active

---

## 12.2 Dry-run renewal

Use this before expiry or if you are unsure:

```bash
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
```

Success:
- dry-run completes successfully
- no DNS or challenge errors

If renewal fails:
- check nginx config
- confirm domain points to `app-1`
- confirm port 80 and 443 are open
- escalate if you cannot fix quickly

---

## 12.3 Manual renewal

Only if needed:

```bash
sudo certbot renew
sudo systemctl reload nginx
```

Verify:

```bash
curl -I https://yourdomain.com
```

Success:
- HTTPS works with valid certificate

---

# 13) nginx operations

## 13.1 Check config syntax

Before reloading nginx:

```bash
sudo nginx -t
```

Success:
- `syntax is ok`
- `test is successful`

## 13.2 Reload nginx safely

```bash
sudo systemctl reload nginx
```

Reload is preferred over restart when possible.

Check status:

```bash
systemctl status nginx --no-pager
```

Success:
- nginx active
- no syntax errors

If nginx will not start, do not keep retrying blindly. Fix the config or revert the change.

---

# 14) PHP-FPM operations

## 14.1 Check status

```bash
systemctl status php8.2-fpm --no-pager
```

## 14.2 Restart if needed

```bash
sudo systemctl restart php8.2-fpm
```

Success:
- service comes back `active (running)`

If restart fails:
- inspect logs

```bash
journalctl -u php8.2-fpm -n 100 --no-pager
```

---

# 15) Uptime Kuma

Uptime Kuma runs on `app-1`.

## 15.1 Check service

```bash
systemctl status uptime-kuma --no-pager
```

If installed as a systemd service, this should work. If not, find the documented service name or process.

## 15.2 What to look for
- monitors are green
- alerts are not firing repeatedly
- Telegram notifications arrive when actual downtime occurs

If Kuma itself is down:
- app monitoring is blind
- restart it only if you know the service name and process
- otherwise escalate

---

# 16) Common incidents and exact response

## 16.1 Site is down

### Step 1: Determine where the failure is
On `app-1`:

```bash
curl -I http://127.0.0.1
curl -I https://yourdomain.com
systemctl status nginx --no-pager
systemctl status php8.2-fpm --no-pager
sudo supervisorctl status
```

On `db-1`:

```bash
systemctl status mysql --no-pager
mysqladmin ping -uroot -p
```

### Step 2: Interpret
- if nginx down: restart or fix config
- if PHP-FPM down: restart PHP-FPM
- if MySQL down: restart MySQL
- if all are up but site still down: check logs

### Step 3: Check logs
```bash
tail -n 100 /var/log/nginx/error.log
journalctl -u php8.2-fpm -n 100 --no-pager
tail -n 100 /path/to/app/storage/logs/laravel.log
```

### When to stop and escalate
Stop if:
- you do not understand the error
- service restarts fail twice
- there is evidence of data loss
- the fix would require code changes you cannot safely make

---

## 16.2 Database is slow

Check:
```bash
top
free -h
df -h
mysqladmin processlist -uroot -p
```

If needed:
```bash
mysql -uroot -p -e "SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST;"
```

Look for:
- long-running queries
- locked tables
- disk full
- memory pressure

Do not kill queries unless you are certain they are safe to stop.

Escalate if:
- many users are affected
- you cannot identify the slow query
- restart seems risky because of active transactions

---

## 16.3 Backup failed

Check:
```bash
crontab -l
grep -i backup /var/log/syslog | tail -n 50
cat /var/log/backup.log
```

Manually run backup script:

```bash
bash /path/to/backup-script.sh
```

If it fails:
- check MySQL credentials
- check disk space
- check rclone config
- check B2 access
- fix only one obvious issue at a time

Stop and escalate if:
- you cannot create a local dump
- you cannot upload to B2
- disk is near full and you do not know what is safe to delete

---

## 16.4 Cert renewal failed

Check:
```bash
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
sudo nginx -t
```

Common causes:
- DNS points elsewhere
- port 80 blocked
- nginx config broken
- challenge path misconfigured

If not obvious, stop and escalate.

---

## 16.5 Disk is almost full

Check:
```bash
df -h
sudo du -sh /var/log/*
sudo du -sh /path/to/app/storage/logs/*
sudo du -sh /tmp/*
```

Common safe actions:
- remove old logs only if you know they are not needed
- clear temporary files
- rotate or compress old application logs if already standard

Do not delete:
- database files
- live application code
- backups you have not copied elsewhere

If unsure, stop and escalate.

---

# 17) Emergency rollback

If a deployment broke production and the issue is clearly related to the release:

## If you use `git pull` directly
Roll back to the previous commit:

```bash
cd /path/to/app
git log --oneline -n 5
git reset --hard PREVIOUS_COMMIT_HASH
composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
php artisan config:cache
php artisan route:cache
php artisan view:cache
sudo systemctl restart php8.2-fpm
sudo supervisorctl restart all
```

Then verify:

```bash
curl -I https://yourdomain.com
```

## If you use release directories
Switch symlink back to the previous release:

```bash
ln -sfn /var/www/releases/PREVIOUS_RELEASE /var/www/current
sudo systemctl reload nginx
sudo systemctl restart php8.2-fpm
sudo supervisorctl restart all
```

Success:
- site returns
- error rate drops
- logs stop showing the new issue

If rollback does not fix it, the incident may not be deployment-related.

---

# 18) Routine maintenance tasks

## Weekly
- check disk usage on both servers
- confirm backup exists and uploads to B2
- check Uptime Kuma dashboard
- review Laravel logs for repeated errors

## Monthly
- run certbot dry-run
- verify MySQL and nginx status
- test restore procedure on a copy if possible in a safe way
- confirm backup retention is still 14 daily copies

---

# 19) Escalation rules

Escalate immediately if:
- you suspect data loss
- MySQL will not start
- backups are failing for more than one day
- certificate renewal is blocked and expiry is near
- nginx config changes break the site
- you are asked to make a change you do not understand
- a command in this runbook behaves differently from expected
- you need to touch firewall, DNS, kernel, or low-level networking and are unsure

Escalation means:
- document what you tried
- copy the exact command output
- notify the business owner or technical lead
- do not keep experimenting in production

---

# 20) What to document after any incident

Write down:
- date and time
- server involved
- symptom
- commands run
- output summary
- fix applied
- whether data was lost
- whether customers were affected

Keep this in a shared doc or incident log.

---

# 21) Minimal command cheat sheet

## app-1
```bash
systemctl status nginx --no-pager
systemctl status php8.2-fpm --no-pager
sudo supervisorctl status
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx
sudo systemctl restart php8.2-fpm
sudo supervisorctl restart all
tail -n 50 /var/log/nginx/error.log
```

## db-1
```bash
systemctl status mysql --no-pager
mysqladmin ping -uroot -p
df -h
crontab -l
rclone ls b2:BUCKET_NAME | tail
bash /path/to/backup-script.sh
```

## TLS
```bash
sudo certbot certificates
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
sudo certbot renew
```

---

# 22) Final notes

Your main job is not to “tune” production. Your main job is to keep it stable, know what normal looks like, and avoid risky changes.

If you are unsure:
1. check service status
2. check logs
3. check disk
4. check backup
5. stop and escalate

That is a good runbook behavior.

If you want, I can turn this into:
- a cleaner Markdown file for the repository,
- a printable one-page emergency cheat sheet,
- or a version with placeholders filled in for your exact paths, domains, and service names.
